results.name: digit_reversal_target_contrast
results.description: Within sets having a two-digit example, yes rate for non-example targets whose digit reversal is an example (e.g. 38 for 83) minus yes rate for other non-example targets of the same sets; observed above null means people use a digit-reversal/same-digits similarity the model lacks, below null means they avoid it more than the model.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_target_contrast
# description: Within sets having a two-digit example, yes rate for non-example targets whose digit reversal is an example (e.g. 38 for 83) minus yes rate for other non-example targets of the same sets; observed above null means people use a digit-reversal/same-digits similarity the model lacks, below null means they avoid it more than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    rev_flag = np.zeros(len(t), bool); ex_flag = np.zeros(len(t), bool); elig = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    cache = {}
    for x in set(s):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        revs = set(int(str(a)[::-1]) for a in v if 10 <= a <= 99 and a % 10 != 0 and a % 11 != 0)
        cache[x] = (set(v), revs)
    ex_sets = [cache[x] for x in s]
    ex_flag = np.array([ti in e[0] for ti, e in zip(t, ex_sets)])
    rev_flag = np.array([ti in e[1] for ti, e in zip(t, ex_sets)])
    elig = np.array([len(e[1]) > 0 for e in ex_sets])
    a = y[elig & rev_flag & ~ex_flag]
    b = y[elig & ~rev_flag & ~ex_flag]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: unstructured_set_nonexample_yes
results.description: Yes rate to non-example targets for multi-example sets with mixed parity, no shared units digit and span of at least 40 (sets fitting no familiar rule or narrow range); observed above null means people generalise more broadly from patternless sets than the model, below null means they are more restrictive.
results.code:
# name: unstructured_set_nonexample_yes
# description: Yes rate to non-example targets for multi-example sets with mixed parity, no shared units digit and span of at least 40 (sets fitting no familiar rule or narrow range); observed above null means people generalise more broadly from patternless sets than the model, below null means they are more restrictive.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.Series(s.unique())
    def props(x):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        par = len(set(a % 2 for a in v))
        units = len(set(a % 10 for a in v))
        return len(v) > 1 and par == 2 and units == len(v) and (max(v) - min(v)) >= 40
    flag = dict(zip(uniq, [props(x) for x in uniq]))
    m = s.map(flag).astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    is_ex = (("," + s + ",").str.contains(",", regex=False)) & pd.Series([("," + a + ",").find("," + b + ",") >= 0 for a, b in zip(s.values, t.values)], index=df.index)
    sel = m & ~is_ex
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float)[sel].mean())

results.name: multi_example_shared_decade_contrast
results.description: In multi-example sets, yes rate for non-example targets sharing a tens digit (decade, 1-9=0s, 100 excluded) with any example minus yes rate for other non-example targets; observed above null means people use decade membership more than the model's ranges and rules imply, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: multi_example_shared_decade_contrast
# description: In multi-example sets, yes rate for non-example targets sharing a tens digit (decade, 1-9=0s, 100 excluded) with any example minus yes rate for other non-example targets; observed above null means people use decade membership more than the model's ranges and rules imply, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cache = {}
    for x in set(s):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        cache[x] = (set(v), set(a // 10 for a in v if a < 100), len(v) > 1)
    ex = np.array([ti in cache[x][0] for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    dec = np.array([(ti < 100) and (ti // 10 in cache[x][1]) for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    multi = np.array([cache[x][2] for x in s])
    a = y[multi & dec & ~ex]
    b = y[multi & ~dec & ~ex]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: mixed_parity_set_even_target_bias
results.description: For sets containing both odd and even examples, yes rate for even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; the model predicts near zero, so observed above null means people carry an even-number preference the model lacks, below null an odd preference.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_set_even_target_bias
# description: For sets containing both odd and even examples, yes rate for even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; the model predicts near zero, so observed above null means people carry an even-number preference the model lacks, below null an odd preference.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cache = {}
    for x in set(s):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        cache[x] = (set(v), len(set(a % 2 for a in v)) == 2)
    ex = np.array([ti in cache[x][0] for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    mixed = np.array([cache[x][1] for x in s])
    even = (t % 2 == 0)
    a = y[mixed & ~ex & even]
    b = y[mixed & ~ex & ~even]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: doubling_relation_target_contrast
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets that are double or half of some example, minus yes rate for other non-example targets of the same sets; observed above null means people generalise along multiplicative (x2) relations more than the model's rule menu predicts, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: doubling_relation_target_contrast
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets that are double or half of some example, minus yes rate for other non-example targets of the same sets; observed above null means people generalise along multiplicative (x2) relations more than the model's rule menu predicts, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cache = {}
    for x in set(s):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        rel = set([2 * a for a in v] + [a // 2 for a in v if a % 2 == 0]) - set(v)
        cache[x] = (set(v), rel)
    ex = np.array([ti in cache[x][0] for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    rel = np.array([ti in cache[x][1] for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    a = y[rel & ~ex]
    b = y[~rel & ~ex]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: prime_target_yes_nonprime_sets
results.description: For sets with no prime example, yes rate for prime non-example targets minus non-prime non-example targets; observed above null means people over-endorse primes (a salient-category bias) the model does not produce, below null means they reject primes more than the model.
results.code:
# name: prime_target_yes_nonprime_sets
# description: For sets with no prime example, yes rate for prime non-example targets minus non-prime non-example targets; observed above null means people over-endorse primes (a salient-category bias) the model does not produce, below null means they reject primes more than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    pr = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cache = {}
    for x in set(s):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        cache[x] = (set(v), not any(a in pr for a in v))
    ex = np.array([ti in cache[x][0] for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    np_set = np.array([cache[x][1] for x in s])
    isp = np.array([ti in pr for ti in t])
    a = y[np_set & ~ex & isp]
    b = y[np_set & ~ex & ~isp]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: single_digit_target_yes_two_digit_sets
results.description: For sets whose examples are all 20 or above, yes rate for single-digit targets (1-9) minus yes rate for other non-example targets; observed above null means people extend to small numbers more than the model, below null means small numbers are rejected more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: single_digit_target_yes_two_digit_sets
# description: For sets whose examples are all 20 or above, yes rate for single-digit targets (1-9) minus yes rate for other non-example targets; observed above null means people extend to small numbers more than the model, below null means small numbers are rejected more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cache = {}
    for x in set(s):
        v = [int(a) for a in x.split(",")]
        cache[x] = (set(v), min(v) >= 20)
    ex = np.array([ti in cache[x][0] for ti, x in zip(t, s)])
    big = np.array([cache[x][1] for x in s])
    small = t <= 9
    a = y[big & small]
    b = y[big & ~small & ~ex]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: target_last_minus_first_example_yes
results.description: In multi-example sets, yes rate when the target equals the last-shown example minus yes rate when it equals the first-shown example; observed above null means people endorse the last example more (recency) than the model's last-example weight implies, below null means they favour the first.
results.code:
# name: target_last_minus_first_example_yes
# description: In multi-example sets, yes rate when the target equals the last-shown example minus yes rate when it equals the first-shown example; observed above null means people endorse the last example more (recency) than the model's last-example weight implies, below null means they favour the first.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    n = parts.str.len()
    first = parts.str[0].astype(int)
    last = parts.str[-1].astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float)
    m = n > 1
    a = y[m & (t == last)]
    b = y[m & (t == first)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())
